title: Runtime Errors
body:
The program compiled, started running, and then died. Nothing was wrong with the *text* of
the program; something was wrong with the state it got into. The compiler cannot catch
these because it does not know what the input will be.

The usual causes in C++:

| Cause | What happens |
|---|---|
| Dereferencing a [[Pointer]] that is `NULL` or garbage | segmentation fault |
| Integer division by zero | crash (floating point division gives `inf`, not a crash) |
| Running off the end of an [[Array]] | undefined behaviour, sometimes a crash, sometimes silent corruption |
| `delete` on a pointer twice, or `delete` on a stack address | heap corruption |
| Unbounded [[Recursion]] | stack overflow |
| Opening a [[File]] that is not there and reading anyway | garbage or a crash |

**C++ does not check array bounds.** `a[100]` on a ten-element array is not a runtime error in
any helpful sense; it reads whatever memory happens to be there. Sometimes it crashes,
sometimes it quietly gives a wrong answer, which turns it into a [[Logic Errors|logic error]]
you cannot see. This is the single biggest difference from Python, where an index error is a
clean exception with a line number.

A crash is the *good* outcome. It means the operating system noticed. [[Assembly Errors]] in
[[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] shows what the hardware is actually reporting when this happens:
bus errors from touching addresses that do not exist, address errors from odd-address word
access, privilege violations from user code reaching into the [[Kernel]].

Finding them: a [[Driver]] with boundary-case inputs (0, 1, empty, the last element) flushes
out most of them, because runtime errors cluster at the edges of the input range. Beyond
that it is `cout` statements or a debugger. See [[debugging]].

The other two thirds of the taxonomy: [[Compile Errors]] stop the build, [[Logic Errors]]
finish and lie. See [[Errors]].
